title: 5.2L Ti-VCT Engine Component Guide
introduction:
I use these drawings to connect the engine’s big assemblies with the smaller pieces hidden inside them. This reference covers the 5.2L 32V Ti-VCT engine: the upper view maps the heads, camshafts, intake and fuel components; the lower view exposes the block, crankshaft, lubrication components and primary timing drive; the piston view brings the piston-to-connecting-rod joint into focus.

Choose the drawing first, follow the leader line from the component to its circled callout, then find the matching Item in that drawing’s table. Each drawing starts its own callout sequence. Read Description together with Part Number, including RH and LH for right-hand and left-hand, intake and exhaust distinctions, quantity notes and any “part of” parent-assembly information. A dash provides no separate part number. The lower table identifies the flywheel for a manual transmission; keep that qualifier attached to the component.

The upper drawing separates the valve covers and camshafts from the heads, with the head gaskets shown at the block joints. The lower drawing places the crankshaft beneath the block and separates its bearing components and caps. The piston drawing then shows how the rings, piston, pin, retainers, connecting rod, bushing and bearing shells relate. I find that last view especially useful: a piston is much easier to understand when its wrist joint is visible instead of disappearing into an aluminum mystery.

Use these views for identification and relationships. Exploded spacing is not a removal sequence or a guide to installation direction. This reference does not specify timing alignment, clearances, tightening values, fastener reuse or inspection limits. Identifying a part is the starting point; work on it requires the matching engine-specific service procedure.

edits.why: The throttle body controls incoming airflow, and the intake manifold distributes that air to the cylinders. The separately illustrated fuel rail and injectors identify the fuel-delivery hardware. At each bank, the cylinder head contains the valves and forms the top of the combustion chambers; its gasket seals the joint to the block. Camshaft lobes operate the valves, so the intake and exhaust labels describe different jobs rather than interchangeable shafts. The secondary chains and their tensioning components belong to the synchronized valve drive. Variable Camshaft Timing (VCT) changes valve-event timing, with intake and exhaust timing controlled independently. I use the separate camshaft, timing-actuator and bearing-cap labels to keep those roles clear. The ignition coil and spark plug are also shown separately, distinguishing the coil-on-plug assembly from the plug beneath it.

The block supports the crankshaft, which receives force through the connecting rods and turns piston travel into rotation. The main bearing shells and caps identify the crankshaft’s support components; the thrust components are separately named, so keep those descriptions distinct. Below them, the oil pan holds the oil reservoir, while the oil pump supplies lubrication passages and the filter captures oil-borne contamination. The filter adapter and cooler are separately identified alongside that hardware. At the front, the primary timing chains, guides, arms and tensioners coordinate crankshaft and camshaft movement. I distinguish that internal timing drive from the external accessory-belt system, and the crankshaft pulley from the crankshaft itself. The VCT variable force solenoids are control components, separate from the camshaft timing actuators shown in the upper view.

This view makes the force path visible: combustion pressure pushes the piston, the connecting rod carries that force, and the crankshaft turns it into rotation. The rings sit around the piston and help seal combustion pressure and control oil along the cylinder wall. The pin connects the piston to the rod’s small end; the drawing separates its retainers and the connecting rod bushing so those pieces can be identified individually. At the rod’s large end, the curved bearing shells identify the bearing at the crankshaft connection. I use the drawing to distinguish the small-end bushing from the large-end bearing, rather than treating every curved insert as the same part. Their separation explains the assembly’s anatomy; ring positioning, fits, clearances and installation methods require the relevant service instructions.
